narratives.narrative: This is a rare inward movement in the family: the self does not resist testing but summons it. The sense (D101 sense, 7696132) is an invitation to God to test the heart; the type (D102 type, 7696133) is volition - not a deed done to another but an act of the will offered up. The bearer (D105 bearer, 7696135) is the psalmist himself, and the operation (D106 operation, 7696136) is precisely the self inviting God to prove, try and test its heart and mind, a confidence willing to be assayed. The target (D107 target, 7696137) is not an enemy but 'confident-self-submission': the movement turns back on the self. The locus (D116 locus, 7696140) confirms this, internal:ib-state - the whole transaction happens inside the inner life even though God is the one addressed. No seat is recorded (D104 seat, 7696134 = none): the offering of heart and mind is not tied to a single organ, a real silence given the heart-language, yet the coupling (D112 coupling, 7696139) binds the operation to 'test-my-heart', so the heart is the thing laid open. Manner is none (D108 manner, 7696138): the psalmist names no dread or reluctance, and that silence itself reads as the calm of integrity. Source is absent (D103), and intensity, specifier and effect are absent (D109/D110/D111), with no prohibition (D113): the text records only the bare, willed act of self-exposure, not its degree or outcome. The discovery note (D114 discovery, 7696141) draws the point out: only an integrity sure of itself asks to be tested. The role (D115 role, 7696142) is characteristic - this willingness-to-be-searched is itself a trait of the inner being. The absences matter as much as the content: no coercion, no resistance, no dread, no stated result - testing here is desired, not endured.
narratives.story: Here a man does something unusual: instead of dreading God's scrutiny, he asks for it. He invites God to prove him, try him, and test his heart and mind. This is entirely an act of his own will, turned back on himself - he is not testing anyone else but laying his own inner life open. The text ties the request to his heart, the thing he wants examined, yet it names no fear, no reluctance, and no single part of him as the place it comes from; the quiet is the point. Nothing is said about how hard the test will be or how it turns out - only that he willingly offers himself. And that willingness is itself the trait on display: only someone confident in his own integrity would ask to be searched.

narratives.narrative: The looking here (D101 sense, 7653358) is raah in its triumphant register - 'my eye has looked in triumph on my enemies'. The type (D102 type, 7653359) is action, and unlike the self-offering of Psa 26 the movement now points outward: the seat (D104 seat, 7653360) is the eye, the bearer (D105 bearer, 7653361) the psalmist, the operation (D106 operation, 7653362) a gaze in triumph, the target (D107 target, 7653363) his enemies. The locus (D116 locus, 7653367) is external:person - the inner state discharges itself upon other people. Crucially the source (D103 source, 7653366) is not the psalmist's own strength but God's act: because God put an end to the enemies (v5). The manner (D108 manner, 7653364) is 'in triumph / vindication', and the coupling (D112 coupling, 7653365) makes the gaze the fruit of God's deliverance - the eye's look is an effect with a divine cause. The discovery note (D114 discovery, 7653368) guards against misreading: this is not gloating cruelty but the settled assurance of God's justice done. Intensity, specifier and effect are absent (D109/D110/D111), and there is no prohibition (D113): the text does not measure the intensity of the look or forbid it, leaving it a bare, vindicated beholding. The role (D115 role, 7653369) is characteristic. Read without valence-bias, the finding is honest about a hard thing - the delivered man looks with satisfaction on his fallen foes - while grounding that satisfaction in God's justice rather than personal spite.
narratives.story: After being rescued, the psalmist says his own eye has looked in triumph on his enemies. This is an outward act - his gaze rests on the people who had hunted his life, now brought down. But the reason he can look this way is not his own power: it is because God put an end to them. So the triumphant look is really the fruit of God's rescue, not personal revenge - the quiet confidence of a man who has seen justice done, not the sneer of someone gloating. The text doesn't dwell on how intense the look is or forbid it; it simply records the vindicated eye of the delivered.
narratives.variation_note: Of the three 'look' readings this one is retrospective and accomplished: the deliverance has already happened (God HAS put an end to the enemies), so the eye looks back in settled triumph on defeated foes - the source dimension records an achieved cause. Contrast look#2 (Psa 59:10), where the same triumphant gaze is still anticipated ('God WILL let me look') and that source is absent, and look#3 (Psa 63:2), where the target shifts entirely from enemies to God beheld in the sanctuary. Same verb, but here the eye rests on people in the past tense of vindication.

narratives.narrative: As in Psa 54, the looking (D101 sense, 7655220) is raah in triumph on enemies, the type (D102 type, 7655221) action, the seat (D104 seat, 7655222) the eye, the bearer (D105 bearer, 7655223) the psalmist, the operation (D106 operation, 7655224) a look in triumph, the target (D107 target, 7655225) his enemies, and the locus (D116 locus, 7655228) external:person. The manner (D108 manner, 7655226) is 'in triumph, by God's grant', and the coupling (D112 coupling, 7655227) grounds it in the God who meets him in his steadfast love (v10). But note the divergence from Psa 54:7: here the source is absent (D103, present:false) - no accomplished cause is recorded, because the deliverance has not yet happened; the gaze is anticipated, not remembered. The discovery note (D114 discovery, 7655229) confirms it: 'God WILL let me look' - the vindicated gaze the delivered psalmist expects. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (D109/D110/D111/D113): the future look is asserted without measure or limit. The role (D115 role, 7655230) is characteristic. The finding lies in the difference: the same trait of triumphant beholding operates in the mode of confident expectation rather than settled fact - trust that the look will come because God's love is coming to meet him.
narratives.story: Here the psalmist looks ahead: he says God will let him look in triumph on his enemies. It is the same kind of gaze as elsewhere - the eye resting in triumph on those who oppose him - but this time it hasn't happened yet. There is no accomplished rescue behind it; instead it rests on the confidence that God, in his steadfast love, is coming to meet him. So the triumphant look is something he expects, not something he already holds. The text sets no limit on it and does not measure it - it simply voices the sure hope that the moment of vindication will arrive.
narratives.variation_note: This 'look' reading is anticipatory where look#1 (Psa 54:7) is accomplished. The key difference is the source dimension: Psa 54:7 records an achieved cause (God HAS put an end to the enemies), but here that source is absent because the looking is still future ('God WILL let me look'). The trait is identical, yet it operates in the mode of expectant trust rather than settled triumph. Both differ from look#3 (Psa 63:2), where the gaze turns from enemies to God.

narratives.narrative: This is the decisive variation within 'look'. The sense (D101 sense, 7656422) is again raah - 'I have looked upon you in the sanctuary' - and the type (D102 type, 7656423) is action, but the target (D107 target, 7656427) is no longer enemies: it is God himself, his power and glory, in the sanctuary. The locus (D116 locus, 7656430) is external:god, not external:person. The bearer (D105 bearer, 7656425) is the psalmist; the operation (D106 operation, 7656426) is to look upon / gaze; the manner (D108 manner, 7656428) is 'beholding his power and glory'. The seat is none (D104 seat, 7656424): this contemplative gaze is not localised in the eye as the triumphant look was - a telling silence, for the beholding of God is not tied to the physical organ. The coupling (D112 coupling, 7656429) is the richest note: this vision is the one that answers the thirst, tying the looking back to the desert-longing of v1 ('my soul thirsts for you'). Source is absent (D103), and intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (D109/D110/D111/D113): the contemplation is recorded without cause, measure or limit. The discovery note (D114 discovery, 7656431) calls it the vision the longing soul feeds on even in the wilderness. Role (D115 role, 7656432) is characteristic. The finding: the same verb that beholds fallen enemies here beholds God, and the movement is satisfied desire rather than vindication - the inner being's gaze turned upward to feed on what it lacks.
narratives.story: This time the looking is turned upward, not outward at enemies. The psalmist remembers gazing on God in the sanctuary, beholding his power and glory. And this looking is set against a raging thirst - in a dry and weary land his soul longs for God, and this vision is the very thing that answers that longing. Unlike the triumphant glance at defeated foes, this gaze isn't pinned to the eye or to any single part of him; it is the whole hungry soul feeding on what it sees. Nothing limits or measures it - it is simply the sight a longing person lives on, even in the desert.
narratives.variation_note: This is the sharpest divergence among the three 'look' readings. Where look#1 (Psa 54:7) and look#2 (Psa 59:10) turn the triumphant eye outward on enemies (locus external:person), here the target and locus shift to God himself (external:god), and the manner changes from triumph/vindication to contemplative beholding that answers a thirst. The same verb carries an entirely different inner movement - satisfied longing rather than vindication - and drops the eye-seat the other two share.

narratives.narrative: This reading inverts the family: seeing appears here as a denied seeing. The sense (D101 sense, 7656759) is raah in the mouth of the wicked - 'Who can see them?' The type (D102 type, 7656760) is status, not action - a settled condition of mind rather than a deed, itself a finding against the active looking elsewhere. The bearer (D105 bearer, 7656762) is the wicked, presuming; the operation (D106 operation, 7656763) is to presume none can see; the locus (D116 locus, 7656767) is internal:ib-state - a movement wholly inside the wicked's interior. Read with no valence-bias (directive 5), this is the descent: the inner being's self-blinding confidence that its scheming is unobserved. The coupling (D112 coupling, 7656766) binds it to the secret snares - the presumption is the interior engine behind the outward plots. Strikingly, target, seat and manner are all 'none' (D107 target 7656764 / D104 seat 7656761 / D108 manner 7656765): the wicked's imagined non-seeing has no object, no organ, no mode - the whole point is that the seeing they deny is empty, aimed at nothing, because they have wrongly ruled it out. Source is absent (D103), and intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (D109/D110/D111/D113). The discovery note (D114 discovery, 7656768) links it to the godless 'who will hear us?' of Ps 59:7 and to God who nonetheless sees and searches the deepest heart (v6-7). Role (D115 role, 7656769) is characteristic. The finding: the same verb that elsewhere beholds God or enemies is here a seeing the wicked cancel in their own minds - the interior presumption of impunity.
narratives.story: This is the dark side of seeing. The wicked, plotting in secret, tell themselves, 'Who can see us?' It is not something they do but a settled state of mind - a confidence, deep inside them, that no one is watching. That presumption is the hidden engine behind their secret traps. And the seeing they deny has no real object at all: they have simply ruled it out, blinding themselves to the fact that God sees and searches even the deepest heart. It is the same word used elsewhere for beholding God, but turned inside out - a self-assured belief that they act unobserved.
narratives.variation_note: The two 'see' readings are opposites. Here (Psa 64:5) seeing is denied and interior: the wicked presume 'who can see them?' - a status of mind (type status), located inside the inner being (internal:ib-state), with no object, seat or manner because the seeing is cancelled. In see#2 (Psa 66:5) seeing is commanded and outward: 'Come and see what God has done' - an action directed at God's deeds (external:god). The same verb runs from godless presumption of impunity to the summons to behold God's works.

narratives.narrative: Here seeing is a summons. The sense (D101 sense, 7658270) is raah - 'Come and see what God has done' - and the type (D102 type, 7658271) is action, a called-for beholding. The bearer (D105 bearer, 7658273) is 'all who are summoned' - not the psalmist alone but a corporate 'come', the widest bearer in the family. The operation (D106 operation, 7658274) is to come and see / behold; the target (D107 target, 7658275) is what God has done; the locus (D116 locus, 7658279) is external:god. The source (D103 source, 7658278) grounds the summons: God is awesome in his deeds (v5) - the seeing is warranted by the works themselves. The coupling (D112 coupling, 7658277) pairs the call to see with the call to 'come and hear' (v16): sight and hearing are the two doors into witnessing God's acts. Seat and manner are none (D104 seat 7658272 / D108 manner 7658276): the beholding is not localised in the eye and no attitude is specified - it is the bare summons to look. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (D109/D110/D111/D113). The discovery note (D114 discovery, 7658280) calls it the corporate counterpart to 'come and hear'. Role (D115 role, 7658281) is characteristic. The finding: seeing here is outward-turned and communal, an invitation for the inner being to be arrested by God's deeds - the exact opposite of the wicked's denied seeing in Psa 64.
narratives.story: Here seeing is an invitation shouted to everyone: 'Come and see what God has done.' It is not one person's private gaze but a call to a whole crowd to look at God's works - and the reason for the call is that those works are awesome. This summons to see runs alongside a matching call later to 'come and hear': looking and listening are the two ways people are brought to witness what God has done. Nothing narrows it to the physical eye or sets any mood; it is simply the open call to behold. It is the bright mirror image of the wicked who told themselves no one could see them.
narratives.variation_note: Opposite to see#1 (Psa 64:5): there seeing is denied, interior and objectless (the wicked presuming none can see); here it is commanded, corporate and outward - an action (not a status) borne by 'all who are summoned' and directed at God's deeds (external:god), warranted by a stated source (God's awesome works). The same verb moves from presumed impunity to a public summons to behold God.

narratives.narrative: This is the family's one instance of self-searching. The sense (D101 sense, 7663544) is chaphas, 'my spirit made a diligent search'; the type (D102 type, 7663545) action. Uniquely, the seat is named and internal: the spirit, ruach (D104 seat, 7663546) - the search is seated in the inmost animating self, and the coupling (D112 coupling, 7663551) reinforces this by pairing the operation with the very spirit that performs it. The bearer (D105 bearer, 7663547) is the psalmist; the operation (D106 operation, 7663548) is to search / examine thoroughly; the manner (D108 manner, 7663550) is diligent, thorough; the locus (D116 locus, 7663552) is internal:ib-state. The target (D107 target, 7663549) is not an enemy or God's deeds but the questions of v7-9 - the search's object is the six anxious questions themselves: has the Lord spurned forever, has his steadfast love ceased, has God forgotten to be gracious? The discovery note (D114 discovery, 7663553) calls it the mind ransacking itself. Source is absent (D103), and intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (D109/D110/D111/D113): the depth of the searching is registered in the manner and seat rather than measured. Role (D115 role, 7663554) is characteristic. The finding: here the inner being turns its searching inward on its own doubts - not God testing man, nor man presuming to test God, but the spirit probing itself to the point of anguished questioning.
narratives.story: Here a troubled man turns his searching inward. Lying awake at night, his own spirit begins a diligent, thorough search - the deep, inmost self ransacking itself. What it searches out is a string of anguished questions: Has the Lord rejected me forever? Has his love run dry? Has God forgotten to be kind? The searching is seated in his very spirit and driven by it, and its whole object is his own doubt. This isn't God probing a person, or a person daring to test God - it is the inner life examining itself, right down to its fears.

narratives.narrative: This begins the run of five 'test' (nasah) readings, all descent. The sense (D101 sense, 7664043) is to test / put to proof; the type (D102 type, 7664044) action; the bearer (D105 bearer, 7664046) 'they', the wilderness generation; the operation (D106 operation, 7664047) to test / try; the target (D107 target, 7664048) God; the locus (D116 locus, 7664051) external:god. This is the inverse of Psa 26:2: there the psalmist invited God to test him; here men presume to test God. The coupling (D112 coupling, 7664050) is decisive - the testing is paired with the heart and the craving: 'they tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved' (D114 discovery, 7664052). So the interior engine is appetite: the test is born of the belly. The seat is none (D104 seat, 7664045) - though the testing is 'in their heart', the row records no organ-seat, a real silence given the heart-language; the coupling, not the seat, carries the heart. Manner is none (D108 manner, 7664049): no mode is named beyond the demand itself. Source, intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (D103/D109/D110/D111/D113). Role (D115 role, 7664053) is characteristic. The finding: testing God here is presumption driven by craving - the inner being demanding proof on its own appetite's terms.
narratives.story: Now the testing runs the wrong way. In the wilderness the people put God to the test - not offering themselves to be examined, but daring to try God. And what drove it was appetite: deep in their hearts they demanded the food they craved, and made their craving a test of whether God could provide. The whole thing is powered by hunger turned into a challenge. It is the mirror image of a person humbly inviting God to search him; this is presumption, the inner self demanding proof on the terms of its own appetite.
narratives.variation_note: First of five 'test' (nasah) readings and the template for the descent. Here the testing is driven by craving - the coupling ties it to the heart and the demanded food. It differs from test#2 (Psa 78:41), which stresses repetition ('again and again'); from test#3 (Psa 78:56), set after the conquest ('even in the promised land'); and from test#4 (Psa 95:9) / test#5 (Psa 106:14), which retell the same wilderness testing in other psalms. This reading's distinctive is motive: appetite as the engine of the test.

narratives.narrative: The second 'test' reading foregrounds repetition. The sense (D101 sense, 7664307) is nasah; type (D102 type, 7664308) action; bearer (D105 bearer, 7664310) 'they'; target (D107 target, 7664312) God; locus (D116 locus, 7664315) external:god. The operation (D106 operation, 7664311) is not simply to test but to 'test again and again' - the distinctive is iteration, testing turned habitual (D114 discovery, 7664316). The coupling (D112 coupling, 7664314) pairs it with provoking the Holy One of Israel: the repeated testing is of a piece with provocation. Seat and manner are none (D104 seat 7664309 / D108 manner 7664313), and source, intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (D103/D109/D110/D111/D113): the row records the bare, repeated act without organ, mode or measured degree. Role (D115 role, 7664317) is characteristic. The finding, read against test#1: the same testing that began in a single craving-driven demand has here hardened into a pattern - the inner being's presumption become a settled habit of provoking God.
narratives.story: This time the emphasis falls on how often it happened: they tested God again and again. What began as a single demand has hardened into a habit - a settled pattern of provoking the Holy One of Israel. The text doesn't add a new motive or measure the intensity; its whole point is the repetition. The inner presumption that once flared up over food has become a way of life, testing God over and over.
narratives.variation_note: Second 'test' reading; its distinctive against test#1 (Psa 78:18) is repetition - the operation is explicitly 'test again and again', testing turned habitual and paired with provoking the Holy One, where test#1 stressed the craving that drove a single demand. Both share bearer ('they'), target (God) and the external:god locus; the difference is a single flare of presumption hardening into a settled pattern.

narratives.narrative: The third 'test' reading is located after the conquest. Sense (D101 sense, 7664351) nasah; type (D102 type, 7664352) action; bearer (D105 bearer, 7664354) 'they'; operation (D106 operation, 7664355) to test; target (D107 target, 7664356) the Most High God; locus (D116 locus, 7664359) external:god. The coupling (D112 coupling, 7664358) pairs the testing with rebelling and not keeping his testimonies. The distinctive is setting: the discovery note (D114 discovery, 7664360) marks the testing renewed even in the promised land - no longer the hungry wilderness but the settled inheritance, and still they test. Seat and manner are none (D104 seat 7664353 / D108 manner 7664357); source, intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition absent (D103/D109/D110/D111/D113). Role (D115 role, 7664361) characteristic. The finding: the testing persists past every provision - even after being given the land, the inner being's presumption continues, now welded to rebellion and covenant-breaking rather than to appetite.
narratives.story: By now the people are settled in the promised land - every need met - and still they test God. Here the testing is bound up with outright rebellion and with refusing to keep his commands. The striking thing is the setting: not the hungry desert this time, but the land of plenty. Even with everything given to them, the old presumption keeps going. What once rose out of craving has become part of a whole pattern of rebellion.
narratives.variation_note: Third 'test' reading; its distinctive is setting - the testing is 'renewed even in the promised land', after the conquest, and is coupled with rebelling and not keeping God's testimonies, where test#1 (Psa 78:18) was driven by wilderness craving and test#2 (Psa 78:41) by sheer repetition. The presumption persists past every provision; the change of arena (desert to inheritance) is itself the finding.

narratives.narrative: This 'proof' reading uses a different verb - bachan (D101 sense, 7670642), 'put me to the proof' - set in the same Meribah/Massah verse as test#4 below. Type (D102 type, 7670643) is action; bearer (D105 bearer, 7670645) the fathers; operation (D106 operation, 7670646) to put to the proof; target (D107 target, 7670647) God. The distinctive is aggravation: the discovery note (D114 discovery, 7670651) stresses the demand for proof despite the works already seen - 'though they had seen my work'. Testing here is not ignorance seeking evidence but presumption discounting evidence already given. The coupling row (D112 coupling, 7670649) carries the value 'external:god', marking the proof-demand as oriented outward against God; the locus row (D116 locus, 7670650) carries 'paired with the testing', tying this bachan directly to the nasah of the same verse - proof and test are the two verbs of one act. Seat and manner are none (D104 seat 7670644 / D108 manner 7670648); source, intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition absent (D103/D109/D110/D111/D113). Role (D115 role, 7670652) characteristic. The finding: 'putting to the proof' names the same wilderness presumption as 'testing' but sharpens it - proof demanded from a God whose works had already been seen.
narratives.story: This uses a slightly different word - putting God to the proof - but it names the same wilderness rebellion, and it comes in the same breath as the word for testing. What makes it sting is one detail: they demanded proof from God even though they had already seen his works. So this isn't honest doubt looking for evidence; it is presumption brushing aside the evidence already given, and turning the demand outward against God himself. Proof and test here are simply two words for one act.
narratives.variation_note: 'Proof' (bachan) occurs only once, but it stands paired with test#4 (Psa 95:9, nasah) in the very same verse - the base source ties the two by the locus value 'paired with the testing'. Its distinctive over the plain 'test' readings is the aggravation named in the discovery: proof is demanded 'though they had seen my work' - evidence already given is discounted.

narratives.narrative: The fourth 'test' reading is the nasah paired with the bachan just discussed, in the Massah/Meribah recollection of Psa 95. Sense (D101 sense, 7670631) nasah; type (D102 type, 7670632) action; bearer (D105 bearer, 7670634) the fathers; operation (D106 operation, 7670635) to test / put to proof; target (D107 target, 7670636) God. The discovery note (D114 discovery, 7670640) names it 'the presumptuous testing of God in the wilderness, unbelief made trial' - the essence of the whole 'test' family stated plainly: unbelief that turns itself into an experiment on God. The coupling row (D112 coupling, 7670638) carries 'external:god'; the locus row (D116 locus, 7670639) carries 'paired with putting God to the proof' - the mirror of proof#1, binding test and proof as one act. Seat and manner are none (D104 seat 7670633 / D108 manner 7670637); source, intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition absent (D103/D109/D110/D111/D113). Role (D115 role, 7670641) characteristic. The finding, read across test#1-3: here in a different psalm the same wilderness testing is retold and given its clearest interior definition - unbelief made trial - and is explicitly doubled with the verb 'proof'.
narratives.story: Here the same wilderness testing is retold in another psalm, and given its plainest description: the fathers put God to the test - unbelief turned into an experiment on God. It sits side by side with the word for putting God to the proof; the two are really one act. There is no new motive or measure added; the value of this telling is its clarity - it names exactly what all this testing is at heart: a lack of trust that dares to make God prove himself.
narratives.variation_note: Fourth 'test' reading; it retells the wilderness testing of test#1-3 in a different psalm (Psa 95) and is explicitly doubled with 'proof' (proof#1) in the same verse - the locus value reads 'paired with putting God to the proof'. Its distinctive is definitional clarity: the discovery calls it 'unbelief made trial', the family's plainest self-definition, rather than adding a new motive (craving in test#1, repetition in test#2, promised-land setting in test#3).

narratives.narrative: The fifth 'test' reading returns to the craving motif of test#1, now in Psa 106. Sense (D101 sense, 7674918) nasah; type (D102 type, 7674919) action; bearer (D105 bearer, 7674921) the fathers; operation (D106 operation, 7674922) to test / put to proof; target (D107 target, 7674923) God in the desert; discovery (D114 discovery, 7674927) 'put God to the test in the desert - the presumptuous trying of God born of appetite'. The locus row (D116 locus, 7674926) carries 'paired with the craving', the interpretive key: as in Psa 78:18 the test is welded to 'a wanton craving in the wilderness' (v14). The coupling row (D112 coupling, 7674925) carries 'external:god'. Seat and manner are none (D104 seat 7674920 / D108 manner 7674924); source, intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition absent (D103/D109/D110/D111/D113). Role (D115 role, 7674928) characteristic. The finding: this reading closes the loop with test#1 - appetite-driven testing - but Psa 106 adds the outcome the others withheld (v15, 'he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease'), though that consequence sits outside the lexical's own effect dimension, which remains absent. The interior movement itself is craving made into a trial of God.
narratives.story: The last of these testing scenes goes back to hunger as the cause: in the desert the people had a wild craving, and out of that craving they put God to the test. It is the same appetite-driven presumption seen before - desire turned into a demand that God prove himself. In this psalm the story adds what happened next: God gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting sickness with it. The trait itself, though, is the inner move of letting craving harden into a test of God.
narratives.variation_note: Fifth 'test' reading; it closes the loop with test#1 (Psa 78:18) - both weld the testing to craving (the locus value here reads 'paired with the craving') - but retells it in Psa 106 with a stated aftermath in the surrounding verse (God grants the request yet sends wasting disease, v15). It differs from test#2 (repetition), test#3 (promised-land setting) and test#4 (definitional 'unbelief made trial'). Distinctive: appetite as engine, now with the consequence visible in the passage.

narratives.narrative: The final reading is a witnessing seeing. Sense (D101 sense, 7676093) raah; type (D102 type, 7676094) action; bearer (D105 bearer, 7676096) the sailors - a fresh bearer, seafarers rather than the psalmist or the wilderness generation; operation (D106 operation, 7676097) to see; target (D107 target, 7676098) the deeds of the Lord, his wondrous works in the deep. The discovery note (D114 discovery, 7676102) frames it as the sailors' witness of God's power on the sea. narratives.story: The last scene is at sea. Sailors out on the deep water see the deeds of the Lord - his wondrous, and here terrifying, works. What they witness is God's power on the ocean: the text places their seeing right before God raises a storm, so the very works in the deep they behold are the tempest that then tosses them until their courage melts away. Nothing narrows the seeing to the eye or names a mood; it is simply people brought face to face with God's overwhelming power. Like the earlier call to 'come and see what God has done', this is seeing turned toward God - but here what is seen is his might in the storm, the sight that comes just before their nerve fails.
